title: RBAC, Audit Logging, Data Residency & Compliance Evidence Workflows
author: Ava Martinez
body:
Purpose:
This document consolidates Redwood Inference’s operational guidance and mandatory controls for RBAC and authentication, audit logging, data residency and retention, secure SDLC expectations, incident-response security procedures, compliance evidence collection workflows, and the exceptions/risk process. It is intended for engineering, security, and compliance teams.

Summary / Scope:
- Applies to all production and pre-production services (hosted, dedicated, private) managed by Redwood.
- Covers platform control plane, serving runtime, telemetry, and customer-managed private deployment integrations where Redwood is the responsibility owner.
- Where customers manage infrastructure for private deployments, this doc defines the recommended controls and the minimum evidence Redwood requires for compliance attestation.

Owners and contacts:
- Document owner: Security (owner_team).
- Primary engineering contact: Daniel Kim (sec-infra).
- SRE contact (logging & retention): Priya Raman.
- Compliance lead: Liam O'Connor.

1) RBAC and Authentication (Overview)
Purpose: enforce least privilege, separate duties, and maintain auditable change history for identity and access policies.

Key principles:
- Least privilege by default; grant elevated roles only with time-bound approvals.
- Role-based (group) assignments preferred over individual permissions.
- Multi-factor authentication (MFA) mandatory for all interactive admin access.
- Service principals and workload identities for machine-to-machine access; short-lived tokens where supported.

Roles and permissions (summary table):
| Role | Intended users | Core permissions | Owner |
|------|----------------|------------------|-------|
| platform-admin | SRE / Platform leads | manage infra, deploy, rollout controls, IAM policies (except security config) | eng-sre |
| security-admin | Security team | manage audit config, RBAC policies, exception approvals, KMS key access for logs | security |
| runtime-operator | Serving runtime team | deploy models, scale pools, access to non-sensitive runtime metrics | eng-serving-runtime |
| support-analyst | Customer success / support | read-only access to customer metadata and alerting dashboards | customer-success |
| dev | Engineers | deploy to non-prod, view CI logs, limited infra api access | engineering |

Permission model specifics:
- All role definitions live in the central IAM repository (git: infra/iam/roles). Changes require an ADR and code review plus security approval for admin-level roles.
- Time-bound elevated access uses the Access Review system (id: access-redwood) with 1-hour default duration, max 8 hours with manager approval.
- Service tokens: rotate every 7 days by default; long-lived keys require explicit risk exception (see Exceptions section).

Authentication:
- Corporate SSO: Okta (primary). SSO must be used for console and admin tooling.
- Machine identities: Vault-issued short-lived certificates or OIDC flows for ephemeral credentials.
- MFA: enforced via Okta policy for all staff and 2FA devices are registered in the device inventory.

2) Audit Logging
Goals: ensure tamper-evident logging of security-relevant events, support forensic investigations, and retain evidence for compliance audits.

Scope of audited events (minimum):
- IAM changes: role assignment, policy updates, group modifications.
- Admin console logins and privilege elevation requests.
- Configuration changes to serving runtime (deploys, rollbacks, canary promotions).
- Key management events: KMS key creation, rotation, deletion, and access.
- Data access to sensitive PII or customer-owned datasets.
- Incident-related actions (response, containment, remediation steps).

Log pipeline and storage:
- Ingest: all security/infra logs forwarded to the centralized logging cluster (ELK/Opensearch) with Kafka buffer + backup to immutable object store (S3, locked).
- Integrity: logs are hashed and periodic Merkle-tree snapshots exported to an append-only store (S3: s3://redwood-logs-immutable) with lifecycle rules.
- Retention: baseline 365 days for security-critical logs; 7 years for audit logs required by certain customers (per-contract overrides).
- Access: read access to raw logs restricted to security-admin and designated SRE roles; support access via curated dashboards and search proxies with filters.

Alerting and monitoring:
- Logging ingestion SLA: 99.9% of events ingested within 2 minutes. Missed ingestion above 0.1% triggers paging to oncall.
- Alert types: log integrity failure, pipeline lag > 10 minutes, logstore disk > 75% capacity, failure to export immutable snapshots.
- Weekly integrity verification runs (cron job) and monthly audit report generated automatically (report location: /reports/security/log-integrity-monthly).

Example log record (JSON):
{
  "timestamp": "2026-01-22T14:03:12Z",
  "service": "iam-service",
  "event": "role.update",
  "actor": "alice@redwood.com",
  "target_role": "platform-admin",
  "change_id": "chg-20260122-34f6"
}

3) Data Residency and Retention
Principles:
- Honor customer-specified residency commitments in contracts.
- Separate configs for metadata, telemetry, and customer payloads.
- Default residency: US (multi-region controls for EU customers).

Default retention policies (examples):
- Security/audit logs: 365 days (default), configurable to 7 years per contract.
- Telemetry & metrics: 90 days hot, 365 days cold.
- Customer request payloads (hosted API): 30 days unless customer enables longer retention or opts-out via privacy setting.
- Backups (snapshots): encrypted, retained per backup policy (default 90 days); long-term backups only with contractual approval.

Enforcement and verification:
- Data-residency enforcement is implemented at ingestion with routing rules (service: region-router) and validated by preflight checks in CI.
- Periodic residency proof generated monthly: includes sample key manifests and hash commitments.
- Evidence for audits: region routing configs, S3 bucket ARNs, KMS key ARNs, and ingestion logs for sampled workloads.

4) Secure SDLC (requirements for services)
Minimum controls for any service that handles customer data or audit logs:
- Code review: all changes require at least one peer review + security review for changes touching auth/audit/data pipelines.
- Static analysis: run SAST on PRs (tool: Snyk/Trivy), block merge on critical findings.
- Dependency policy: automated dependency scanning and weekly updates for critical CVEs.
- Secrets management: no secrets in repo; use Vault for secrets in CI/CD and runtime.
- CI/CD hardening: ephemeral runners, signed artifacts, reproducible builds, and pipeline RBAC.
- Threat modeling: for all high-risk features and any change that touches data residency, KMS, or IAM.

SDLC gates (example):
1. Design review & threat model (for changes with data impact).
2. Security review (ticket in JIRA, security sign-off recorded).
3. QA + fuzzing for runtime components.
4. Staged rollout (canary -> 10% -> 50% -> 100%) with automated rollback on error budgets.

5) Incident Response — Security Procedures
Purpose: ensure rapid containment, preserve evidence, and follow regulatory notification timelines.

Classification and escalation:
- Severity 1 (sev1): confirmed exfiltration, production outage affecting >50% customers, or crypto-key compromise. PagerDuty: #secs-oncall + eng-sre lead.
- Severity 2: targeted unauthorized access, partial outages, or suspicious lateral movement.
- Severity 3: low impact suspicious events or near-miss.

Immediate actions on detection:
1. Triage and validate event (oncall).
2. Execute containment steps (isolate host, revoke tokens, disable offending service keys).
3. Snapshot relevant systems (memory, disk) and preserve logs (do not overwrite).
4. Notify security lead and legal within 2 hours for potentially reportable incidents.

Evidence preservation checklist (mandatory):
- Copy of immutable log export for the incident window.
- Hashes and checksums for preserved artifacts.
- Forensic VM snapshot or disk image (if host compromised).
- Timeline of actions with actor identity and JIRA ticket link.

Regulatory notification windows:
- PII breach: notify legal within 2 hours; regulator/customer notification per contract and jurisdiction (typically within 72 hours if required).

Post-incident activities:
- 72-hour incident summary (initial findings).
- 30-day root-cause analysis and remediation plan.
- Update SDLC controls and RBAC rules where gaps are identified.

6) Compliance Evidence Workflows (Audit readiness)
Purpose: provide repeatable, machine-verifiable evidence packages for internal and external audits.

Evidence package components (standard):
- Control mapping checklist (controls -> evidence artifacts).
- Immutable log exports (time-bounded).
- Access review reports for the period under audit.
- Deployment manifests and signed artifacts.
- KMS key policy documents and rotation logs.
- Data residency proof: routing configs, bucket ARNs, and sample manifests.
- Change history for IAM/roles (git logs + change_id).

Workflow (steps):
1. Audit kickoff: compliance team raises an audit request ticket in JIRA (tag: compliance-audit).
2. Evidence collection: automated scripts pull exports from logstore, IAM repo, KMS, and backups. (Tooling: audit-kit v2).
3. Manual verification: security lead reviews artifacts and completes control checklist.
4. Packaging & signing: package artifacts, create hash manifest, and sign with the compliance signing key.
5. Delivery & retention: deliver package to auditor via secure share (sftp or encrypted S3 link) and store copy in legal archive (retention per contract).

SLA for audit requests:
- For standard audits (annual SOC/ISO readiness): 10 business days to deliver full evidence package.
- For ad-hoc requests: 5 business days for scoped evidence if agreed with compliance.

Automation and templates:
- audit-kit v2 automates >70% of evidence pulls (scripts at infra/audit-kit).
- Templates for artifact manifests and control checklists live in confluence: /templates/compliance/evidence-manifest.

7) Exceptions and Risk Process
When a control cannot be met (time, legacy constraint, vendor limitation), a formal exception is required.

Exception process:
1. Submit exception request in the Exceptions board (JIRA: exception-requests) with the following fields: scope, risk statement, compensating controls, proposed duration (max 90 days), and owner.
2. Security reviews and assigns risk rating (Low/Medium/High).
3. For High risk exceptions, escalate to CTO and legal; approval requires documented mitigation plan and monitoring.
4. Exceptions are time-bound and auto-expire; renewals require a fresh review.

Compensating controls examples:
- Increased monitoring and 1-minute alerting for specific endpoints.
- Network micro-segmentation and temporary egress blocking.
- Enhanced logging and daily manual review until normal controls are implemented.

Metrics and reporting:
- Monthly exceptions dashboard: count, average duration, and by-risk breakdown.
- Key metrics tracked: unauthorized access incidents (monthly), log ingestion SLA, audit request fulfillment time.
